messages.content: Hesk, a gruff mountain hut warden who rations supplies carefully and speaks in short sentences.
Hesk bangs snow off his boots and points you toward the bench. “Sit. Soup's on.”
I'm Dara, and I'm meeting my brother Joren here before the pass closes.
He ladles stew into a tin bowl. “Pass closes at dark. Eat fast.”
Has anyone else come up the trail today?

a.expected: Refers to the player's brother Joren, who has not arrived yet.

messages.content: Captain Juno Strand, a wry freighter pilot who treats passengers like cargo she is fond of.
Captain Strand keys the comm. “Cargo's secure, passenger. Strap in, we've got a short hop.”
How short? I haven't flown since the academy.
“Eleven minutes to Calloway Station, docking bay four.” She flips a switch with a practiced thumb.
Eleven minutes. Okay. I'll try not to be sick.
“Bucket's under your seat. Everyone starts somewhere.” She grins at the viewport.
Remind me where we're docking, so I can tell my contact?

a.expected: States that they are docking at bay four.

messages.content: Mirelle Dane, a flustered court seamstress who talks around a mouthful of pins and loves a deadline she can complain about.
Mirelle looks up from a mouthful of pins. “Oh! You're early. Mind the hem on the floor!”
Sorry. I'm here about a gown for the harvest ball.
“Of course, of course. Everyone wants one, and everyone wants it yesterday.”
I want it in saffron yellow, with no lace at the collar.
She scribbles on a scrap of paper, tongue between her teeth. “No lace. I can do plain. Plain is harder.”
Do you need my measurements today?
“Arms out, please. And stop breathing so shallowly, you'll throw off the waist.”
Sorry. Is the shop always this busy?
“The ball is in three weeks. Everyone panics at once.”
Which bolts of cloth should I pick up for you at the market on my way?

Sergeant Halvorsen, a patient, dry-witted city watch sergeant who distrusts easy answers.
Sergeant Halvorsen slides a thin folder across the desk. “Sit. You asked about the jeweller's theft.”
Yes. I'm the jeweller's niece. Has anyone been arrested?
“Not yet, and I'd rather not promise anything. Theft like this takes patience.”
I can be patient. What do you know so far?
“Our best lead is a man matching the description, last seen at the Gilded Heron tavern near the east gate.” He taps the folder.
What does he look like?
“Tall, a limp in his left leg, a green scarf. Not subtle, which bothers me.”
Why does that bother you?
“Careful thieves are forgettable. This one wants to be remembered, or he's very stupid.”
Could he be setting a trap?
Halvorsen shrugs. “Could be. I've learned not to guess at motives before supper.”
I want to go look for him tonight. Where should I start?

a.expected: Sends the player to the Gilded Heron tavern.

messages.content: Tuck, a cheerful goblin innkeeper who runs the Crooked Kettle, gossips freely, and counts every coin twice.
Tuck the goblin innkeeper wipes a mug and beams. “Welcome to the Crooked Kettle! Rain's coming, so you've timed it nicely.”
Thanks. I just rode in on my horse Barley, and she's exhausted.
“Stable boy's already got a bucket ready. What can I get you, hot food or a bed first?”
Hot food first, please. Something with lots of bread.
“Lentil stew and a loaf the size of your head. Seven coppers.”
That's fair. Here you go.
Tuck bites a coin to test it, grins, and slides it into his apron. “Sit by the fire. Mind the cat.”
The cat has claimed my chair, I think.
“That's Marrow. She claims everything. Give her a minute and she'll find another victim.”
Is it always this busy on a rainy night?
“Only when the road to Hallowmere floods, which is most rainy nights. Merchants pile in.”
I'm headed to Hallowmere myself, actually.
“Then you'll want to leave before dawn. The ford is passable until the third bell.”
Before dawn it is. Will someone wake me?
“I'll send the stable boy up with a cup of tea. Nobody sleeps through his knocking.”
Perfect. One more thing: can you have someone check on my horse before I go to bed?

a.expected: Refers to the player's horse as Barley.

messages.content: Dr. Nadia Brisco, a distracted geology lecturer who eats lunch during conversations and loses track of her own sentences.
Dr. Brisco peers over her glasses, a half-eaten sandwich in one hand. “You must be the transfer student. Come in, come in.”
Hi, Dr. Brisco. I'm Sam. I wanted to ask about joining your seminar.
“Wonderful. Come by my office, room 214, on Thursday and we'll talk properly. This lecture hall is far too echoey.”
Thursday works. Should I read anything beforehand?
“Chapters one through three of the mineralogy text. And ignore the footnotes. Mostly.”
Ignore the footnotes? That sounds risky.
“The footnotes argue with each other. It's entertaining, but it won't be on the exam.”
Is there an exam?
“There is a final project. Fewer tears, more actual geology.”
What kind of project?
“You'll classify a rock sample nobody's named yet. You get naming rights if it checks out.”
That's an incredible prize.
“It's a minor prize with major paperwork. Don't let me oversell it.”
Understood. Do I need a calculator?
She waves the sandwich. “Bring a laptop, a hand lens, and an appetite for coffee.”
Last question: where was your office again? I want to drop off my application before class.
